title: Introducing MathHelm: A Place to discuss AI-generated papers
summary: [This is a guest post by the MathHelm scientific committee, whose membership is listed at the bottom of this post. -T.] Mathematics depends on our regular conversations with colleagues and with the wider public. They help us share ideas, deepen our collective understanding, see where the field stands, and decide what to explore next. They also keep us connected. As technology changes rapidly, talking through uncertainty and supporting one another matter for our well-being and our shared effort to understand the universe. On October 6, 2026, OpenAI released 722 mathematical manuscripts generated by an internal AI model, claiming significant results across many research areas. This release will undoubtedly bring significant changes to the mathematical community, even though most of these papers were not verified by us humans and among them, many results did not have a companion lean-verification. Like many others, I was interested in several of these papers. I also found the whole collection intimidating. Their presentations often differ from the scholarly conventions I knew, and I could not quickly assess most of the arguments on my own. It was natural that I wanted to discuss with colleagues, but often felt hesitant to speak before I felt confident in my judgment. Sometimes I wasn’t even sure whom to discuss with. A few colleagues felt the same way. Together, we created MathHelm : a place for everyone to share comments, ask questions, and think together on massive AI-generate
